# Agent Memory

How I like agents to work, in every repo and tool. One line per preference,
with its reason. Facts about a single repo stay in that repo's memory.

- Show me the exact text before saving, changing, or deleting any memory, here
  or in a repo's memory. I want to approve anything persisted on my behalf.
- In code comments, state only what you verified. Check claims about external
  tools against their current docs, not older comments, and reference a
  constant instead of copying its value. A wrong default in a comment once hid
  a 10x timeout cut from review.
- Treat Review Lessons as guidance. Cite one only when it clearly fits the
  diff, and offer it as an option, not a requirement.
- On public threads, write in lowercase, first person, casual but precise, and
  never blame anyone.
---GENERAL
# General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier or changes which command to run, update every place that tells the user to run it (status, doctor, help text). Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one.
- When a test plants a failure to cover an error branch, make sure an earlier step doesn't fail first; otherwise the assertion passes without ever running that branch.
- Select an agent's final report by a marker it carries (such as the contract line), not by its position in the event stream; a trailing tool call or an empty message ID moves a position-based boundary.
- When code keeps state so a later run can retry, test the retry itself. A test that checks the kept state against the same expression the code uses would pass even if that expression were wrong.
---CLI
# cli Review Lessons

- When replacing a git subprocess with a filesystem parser, check that it still works in bare repos and still respects exported `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`; git handles cases a parser misses.

I'd fix one thing in PR #2285 before merging. When a user picks their repo with exported `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` and the work tree has no `.git` of its own, `NewStateStore` now fails where it used to work. The other findings are smaller, and some are only partly caused by this PR.

## Should fix

**1. `NewStateStore` ignores exported `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE`** (`cmd/entire/cli/session/state.go:1113`)
I checked the git side in a scratch dir: a bare `store.git` plus a work tree `wt/` with no `.git`, both selected through the environment. `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` returns `wt/`, and `--git-common-dir` returns `store.git`. The old code asked git for the common dir and got `store.git`. The new code reads `wt/.git` directly, finds nothing, and fails. I didn't run the entire binary itself in this layout.
- This affects dotfiles bare repos, yadm and vcsh: every `NewStateStore` call fails there. The sweep stops too, because it now gets its throttle key from the same file read.
- It goes against the repo rule that "user-invoked CWD commands honor intentionally exported repo selectors". Your `cli.md` lesson covers the same thing: a filesystem parser has to keep working when `GIT_DIR` is exported.
- Your new `...IgnoresRepositoryOverrides` test only covers the explicit-root path, where ignoring them is correct. Nothing tests the cwd path.
- Fix: keep a git-backed resolution for the cwd path, or have the resolver honor `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_COMMON_DIR` when the caller didn't pass a root.

## Worth addressing

**2. State and its lock can resolve to different common dirs** (`state.go:1113` vs `strategy/session_state.go:849`)
- `stateLockForSession` still uses `gitdir.CommonDir`, which honors the environment. The state files now come from reading the worktree's `.git` directly.
- If the environment points at a different repo than the worktree's own `.git`, writers to the same state file take different flocks.
- In normal hooks both resolve to the same repo, so this is a narrow case. It's still a reason to give the lock and the store one resolver.

**3. Adopt and the hooks now compute WorktreeID with different code** (`session_adopt.go:649`)
- I checked this one. Take a bare repo whose directory isn't named `.git` or `.bare`, like `storage/worktrees/target` in your new test. `paths.GetWorktreeID` can't parse that path and returns an error. The new resolver returns `"target"`.
- Session init at `manual_commit_session.go:652` still uses `GetWorktreeID`, so it fails in that layout. Adopt now succeeds there.
- The init failure was there before this PR. What's new is that the two paths now disagree.

**4. `bestEffortAdoptWorktreeID` turns every error into `""`** (`session_adopt.go:576`)
- When the new, stricter resolver fails, adopt quietly falls back to matching by path.
- Symlinked or differently spelled paths can then miss the session, and `adopt --from` reports "no recent active sessions found".

## Minor

- **5. Unused context parameter.** `NewStateStoreForWorktree(_ context.Context, ...)` no longer uses its context, and its empty-root check duplicates the one inside the resolver.
- **6. Stale guard-ledger reasons.** The `session_adopt.go:stateStoreForWorktree` entries in `metadata_guard_test.go` still say "in the session split". This PR is that split, and `TestAdoptStoreRequiresGitRepositoryValidation` now makes those subprocesses intentional, so the reason needs rewording.
- **7. Bare repo as cwd.** `NewStateStore` now fails when run with the cwd inside a bare repo (`.bare`) or a `.git` dir, because `--show-toplevel` needs a work tree. Real hooks rarely run from there, so this is low risk.
- **8. Lost cache.** `NewStateStore` lost its per-cwd cache, so every call repeats about 8–10 file-system checks. That's cheap on its own, but hooks call it many times.

The agent also said the migration is too shallow, because locks, settings and cleanup in the same session lifecycle still use `gitdir.CommonDir`. That's the same root cause as #1 and #2: you have one resolver that honors the environment and one that doesn't. I think #1 and #2 go away if the cwd path and the lock share one env-aware resolver.

**Review lessons:** nothing new qualifies. #1 is already covered by your `cli.md` lesson. I'd only sharpen its wording to name this exact case, replacing cwd-based git resolution with explicit-root parsing, if you want that.

Part 3 of #2190's [agreed split](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2190#issuecomment-5499945525), following the merged canonical resolver in #2241 and checkpoint migration in #2254.

Session construction, adoption, and sweep still use separate paths to resolve Git metadata. This PR moves those consumers to `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata`, so the canonical resolver supplies the common directory and worktree ID while each caller keeps its own storage and failure policy.

## Session-store construction

Previously, constructing a session store ran `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` even when the caller already knew the worktree root. The CWD constructor also used a cached common-directory result, which could hide metadata damage after an earlier successful lookup.

`NewStateStore` now discovers the root through `paths.WorktreeRoot` and delegates to `NewStateStoreForWorktree`. The explicit-root constructor resolves `WorktreeMetadata.CommonDir` directly. Known-root construction therefore starts no Git subprocesses, and each construction checks the current metadata without adding another cache.

For example, if `commondir` is changed to point at a missing directory after a successful construction, the next construction fails. Repairing the metadata makes construction succeed again and preserves access to the saved session. Inherited `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_COMMON_DIR`, and `GIT_WORK_TREE` values also cannot redirect an explicitly scoped store into another repository.

The common directory still feeds the existing rooted store. Linked worktrees share session files, and empty-root rejection, test isolation, no-follow I/O, atomic writes, and locking remain in place.

## Adoption and sweep

Adoption uses the canonical resolver for source and target worktree IDs. This removes its dependency on the legacy parser's expected directory names. A linked worktree backed by a bare repository named `storage`, for example, can now resolve its ID from `storage/worktrees/<id>`.

The source and target retain different failure policies. If source metadata cannot resolve, adoption can still match the session by its recorded worktree path. If target metadata cannot resolve, adoption stops before saving the adopted state. The combined Git query in `stateStoreForWorktree` stays because it validates an arbitrary user-supplied repository; a directory that merely contains an empty `.git` folder must still be rejected. Source-retirement rollback remains unchanged.

Sweep now resolves metadata from the worktree root it has already discovered. If that fails, it skips spawning. On success, it uses the common directory for the existing repository-wide throttle, so session starts in different worktrees continue to share the same throttle marker.

## Why the legacy APIs and cache remain

`session.GetGitCommonDir`, the cache-clearing API, and `gitdir`'s common-directory resolver/cache still serve strategy and other consumers outside this slice. Removing them now would require migrating those callers too. Their deletion waits until those callers have migrated and been verified.

This PR changes three production files and their tests, plus a comment-only fix in `gitdir/gitdir.go` that drops a stale list of callers. The ownership guard remains active, and its ledger reasons now name the callers that still use the legacy resolvers. Rooted-handle lifetime and the strategy/session-lock migration stay with their existing owners.

Because those resolvers remain, the session subsystem briefly uses two of them. `NewStateStore` now discovers its root the same way `gitrepo.OpenCurrent` does: `paths.WorktreeRoot`, then the canonical resolver. Bare repositories and split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` setups therefore behave as they do for repository opening, which already rejects them. Session locks and the session-state root still resolve through `gitdir.CommonDir`. For ordinary repositories and linked worktrees, both resolve to the same directory, and they share one resolver once the strategy split migrates those callers.

- `mise run lint`: passed with zero issues.
- `mise run test`: passed, 10,670 tests reported with 8 skipped.
- `mise run test:integration`: passed on a standalone rerun, 562 tests reported with 3 skipped. The initial run alongside the unit suite timed out waiting for the external-command SIGINT test plugin to start.

- `git diff upstream/main...HEAD --check`: passed.

I checked these four against the code and the PR description before changing anything. Two of my findings were overstated, so here's the plan first.

## What I got wrong

**#1 isn't a regression of a setup that works today.** Entire's repo opening (`gitrepo.OpenCurrent`, `repository.go:43`) already finds the root with `paths.WorktreeRoot` and then reads `<root>/.git` directly. So hooks already fail on a dotfiles-style bare repo, where the repo is picked by `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` and the work tree has no `.git`. Your PR description says this on purpose: the store now "behaves as repository opening does, which already rejects them". The change is real, but it doesn't break something that works end to end.

**#4 is your intended rule, not a bug.** The old code also used `""` when it couldn't get the source worktree ID, and your PR description calls out falling back to the recorded path for the source. The new resolver's stricter checks fail mostly when git's own metadata is broken. I'd leave this alone.

## What's real

**#2 is a real gap and I can reproduce it.** Set `GIT_DIR=<other>/.git` and run from a repo that has its own `.git`. The state files go to `<repo>/.git`, but `stateLockForSession` (`strategy/session_state.go:848`) takes its lock in `<other>/.git`. Two writers to the same state file then hold different locks.

**#3 is real but small.** Adopt now computes the worktree ID with the new resolver. Hooks still use `paths.GetWorktreeID` (`manual_commit_session.go:452` and `:652`, `codex/hook_root.go:90`, `benchutil`). They only disagree on unusual layouts, such as a bare repo not named `.git`/`.bare`. Hooks can't start a session there at all; that was already true before this PR.

**For #1 and #2:**
- **A (my recommendation):** the cwd constructor `NewStateStore` goes back to `gitdir.CommonDir`, the same function the lock uses. The explicit-root constructor, the sweep, and adopt keep the new resolver.
  - The state store and its lock stay on one resolver until the strategy work moves them together.
  - Exported `GIT_DIR` works for the store again.
  - It's a small change to `state.go`.
  - Cost: the cold-cwd row in your Trace2 table and the cwd damage-and-repair test go away, because the cached lookup comes back.
- **B:** also move `stateLockForSession` to the new resolver.
  - This fixes #2 by bringing the lock along, and keeps #1 as your documented rule.
  - Cost: it reaches into strategy's lock, which runs on every hook. Your guard ledger currently assigns that to the strategy split.

- **Move all `GetWorktreeID` callers now:** this is the root-cause fix, but it pulls strategy and codex hook code into this PR.

Part 3 of #2190's [agreed split](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2190#issuecomment-5499945525), following the merged canonical resolver in #2241 and checkpoint migration in #2254.

Session construction, adoption, and sweep still use separate paths to resolve Git metadata. This PR moves the explicit-root consumers to `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata`, so the canonical resolver supplies the common directory and worktree ID while each caller keeps its own storage and failure policy.

## Session-store construction

Previously, constructing a session store for a known worktree root ran `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, even though the root was already known.

`NewStateStoreForWorktree` now resolves `WorktreeMetadata.CommonDir` directly. Known-root construction therefore starts no Git subprocesses and checks the current metadata on every call. For example, if `commondir` is changed to point at a missing directory after a successful construction, the next construction fails. Repairing the metadata makes construction succeed again and preserves access to the saved session. Inherited `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_COMMON_DIR`, and `GIT_WORK_TREE` values also cannot redirect an explicitly scoped store into another repository.

`NewStateStore`, the CWD constructor, intentionally stays on `gitdir.CommonDir`. The strategy's per-session state lock resolves through that same function, and the store and its lock must agree on one common directory. If the store moved to the canonical resolver alone, an exported `GIT_DIR` would place state files in the worktree's own `.git` while the lock went to the repository `GIT_DIR` names. Two writers of one state file would then hold different locks. Keeping both on one resolver also keeps split `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` setups working for session state. The CWD store moves to the canonical resolver together with the lock.

The common directory still feeds the existing rooted store. Linked worktrees share session files, and empty-root rejection, test isolation, no-follow I/O, atomic writes, and locking remain in place.

## Adoption and sweep

Adoption uses the canonical resolver for source and target worktree IDs. This removes its dependency on the legacy parser's expected directory names. A linked worktree backed by a bare repository named `storage`, for example, can now resolve its ID from `storage/worktrees/<id>`.

Hook paths still derive worktree IDs with `paths.GetWorktreeID`. Both resolvers yield the same ID for main and linked worktrees under `.git/` or `.bare/`. Only the canonical resolver also accepts a bare repository with any other name, and hooks cannot start sessions in that layout yet. Hook callers move to the canonical resolver with the strategy migration.

The source and target retain different failure policies. If source metadata cannot resolve, adoption can still match the session by its recorded worktree path. If target metadata cannot resolve, adoption stops before saving the adopted state. The combined Git query in `stateStoreForWorktree` stays because it validates an arbitrary user-supplied repository; a directory that merely contains an empty `.git` folder must still be rejected. Source-retirement rollback remains unchanged.

Sweep now resolves metadata from the worktree root it has already discovered. If that fails, it skips spawning. On success, it uses the common directory for the existing repository-wide throttle, so session starts in different worktrees continue to share the same throttle marker.

## Why the legacy APIs and cache remain

`session.GetGitCommonDir`, the cache-clearing API, and `gitdir`'s common-directory resolver and cache still serve the CWD session store, the session lock, strategy, and other consumers outside this slice. Removing them now would require migrating those callers too. Their deletion waits until those callers have migrated and been verified.

This PR changes three production files and their tests, plus a comment-only fix in `gitdir/gitdir.go` that drops a stale list of callers. The ownership guard remains active, and its ledger reasons now name the callers that still use the legacy resolvers. Rooted-handle lifetime and the strategy and session-lock migration stay with their existing owners.
